1 · What the Audit Ledger is

The Audit Ledger is an append-only, tamper-evident record of what Tracelane's gateway did on your behalf: every AI-provider request it proxied and every guardrail or eval verdict it produced. Each entry is written once and never changed. Entries are cryptographically linked together, so if anyone alters, removes, or reorders even a single past entry, the change becomes provable — not just to Tracelane, but to any independent party.

The one-sentence version
It is a sealed logbook for your agents: you can show an auditor exactly what ran, and mathematically demonstrate that the log was not edited after the fact.

What it is not: it is not your full trace data. Rich, full-fidelity spans (prompts, tool calls, timings) live on the Traces page. The Audit Ledger is the smaller, sealed evidence record — the part designed to stand up to scrutiny.

2 · Why it matters

If you are…The Audit Ledger gives you…
A developerA trustworthy history of what your agents actually did in production — no “trust me” logs that could have been quietly edited.
An ops / on-call engineerAn incident-grade record: when something goes wrong, the sequence of events is fixed and verifiable.
A compliance / risk officerEvidence you can hand to an auditor or regulator (e.g. under the EU AI Act’s record-keeping expectations) that is independently verifiable without trusting the vendor.
A customer of yoursAssurance you can demonstrate what your AI did on their behalf, and prove the record is genuine.

3 · How it works (in plain terms)

Two mechanisms work together. You do not need to understand the math to trust the result — but here is what is happening.

a. The hash chain — tamper-evidence

Every entry gets a fingerprint (a SHA-256 hash) computed from its contents. Each entry also carries the fingerprint of the entry before it — like each page of a ledger citing the exact wording of the previous page. Change any past entry and its fingerprint changes, which breaks the link to the next entry, and to every entry after it. So a single silent edit is impossible to hide: re-computing the fingerprints exposes exactly where the break is.

Who cares, concretely?
An auditor asks “how do I know this log wasn’t cleaned up before you showed me?” The hash chain is the answer: they re-compute the fingerprints themselves and see that every link holds — or see precisely which entry was tampered with.

b. Public anchoring — independent, third-party proof

Your entries are grouped into batches (about 100 events each). For each batch, a single summary fingerprint (a Merkle root) is published to Sigstore’s public transparency log — an append-only, tamper-evident log run by the open-source community, independent of Tracelane. This is like getting a notary’s timestamp on each batch. Because the proof lives in a public log Tracelane does not control, it demonstrates your records existed, in that exact form, at that time — even if you stopped trusting Tracelane entirely.

Anchoring runs from your ledger’s very first entry (its genesis) onward. One anchor is published per batch, so the number of anchors grows as your ledger grows.

4 · The page, section by section

Open Audit from the top navigation. Here is what you see and what each part means.

The trust panel & “Verify integrity”

This is the dominant panel at the top. Before you verify, it shows a neutral Ready to verify state explaining what the check does. The single orange Verify integrity button runs the check.

“About this ledger” — scope, anchoring & retention

A supporting panel that states what the ledger covers, its Public anchoring count (batches anchored within the events shown), and its Retention — the ledger is append-only and never expires, unlike your plan’s trace-retention window.

Why the anchoring number can look “small”
The page loads a fast, verifiable preview (the first ~1,000 events from genesis). If your ledger has, say, 2,500 events across 25 batches, the preview contains the first 10 batches — so you’ll see “10 anchored”. That is not a cap on your ledger; the complete ledger (all 25 batches) is in the export. The preview is sized so the in-browser check stays instant even for very large ledgers.

The hash chain

A visual walk of the entries, newest linkage highlighted, ending in the chain head (the fingerprint of the latest loaded entry). Expand any row to see exactly the data its fingerprint covers — full transparency into what is being hashed.

5 · Walkthrough: verify integrity

1
Open the Audit page. The trust panel shows “Ready to verify”.
2
Click “Verify integrity”. The verifier — open-source code — runs entirely in your browser. Nothing is sent to Tracelane; nothing is taken on trust.
3
Read the verdict. Within a moment you get a plain-English result and a two-claim breakdown (below). A green result is one you reproduced.
Why “in your browser” matters
The check does not ask Tracelane “is this valid?” and trust the answer. It re-does the math locally over data you can inspect. That is what makes it credible evidence rather than a vendor claim.

6 · Reading the result

The verdict is deliberately split into two claims, never one blurred “OK”, so you always know exactly what was proven.

ClaimPlain meaning
Claim 1 — what we recomputed (Hash chain)The verifier re-computed every entry’s fingerprint and every link between entries, locally. If this is green, your records are intact and in order.
Claim 2 — what the public log proves (Signature & public anchor)Your batch fingerprints were signed by your key and found in Sigstore’s public log, checkpoint verified — independent, third-party confirmation.

Outcome A — Verified green

The chain is intact, your key’s signature checks out, and at least one batch is confirmed in the public log. This is the strongest state.

Outcome B — Chain verified green (qualified)

The chain is intact and signed, but no public anchor happened to fall inside the on-screen preview (e.g. your newest batch hasn’t been anchored yet). Still tamper-evident — run the export + CLI for the public-log proofs across the whole ledger.

Outcome C — Integrity check failed red

Something does not add up: a fingerprint doesn’t match, a link is broken, or an anchor proof is missing. The page tells you the first failing entry and — importantly — what to do next.

7 · Scenario flows: if this, then that

Verified (green)
You’re done. This is your evidence. For a formal hand-off, download the complete ledger (§8) and archive it — the download is the record an auditor can independently verify.
Chain verified (no anchor in view)
Normal for a very recent or small ledger. If you need public-log proof now, download the complete ledger and run tlane verify — it checks every batch, including ones outside the on-screen preview.
Failed — first time
Re-download a fresh copy from “Download the complete ledger” and verify again. Most failures are a downloaded file that was edited or truncated locally — a fresh export clears that.
Failed — fresh export still fails
Treat it as a potential integrity incident. Email support@tracelane.dev with the first failing seq (shown on the page) and the export attached. Nothing in the app can “fix” a broken chain by design — that is exactly what tamper-evidence is for.
No events yet
The ledger starts with your first gateway-proxied call. Point an agent at the Tracelane gateway and entries appear here.

8 · Getting the complete ledger

The on-screen chain is a fast preview. The complete, uncapped ledger — the file an auditor verifies — is the export. On the Audit SKU this is a one-click download; on other plans you can see and verify your preview for free, and the downloadable evidence pack is the paid add-on.

Free vs. paid
Free on every plan: see your chain from genesis, run the in-browser “Verify integrity”, read both claims. Audit SKU add-on: download the complete, uncapped evidence pack and verify it offline with the tlane verify command-line tool — the format built for regulator hand-off. The Compliance & Evidence Handbook (available to Audit-SKU customers) covers that end-to-end.

9 · Glossary

Tamper-evident
Changes cannot be hidden. Altering a record doesn’t become impossible — it becomes detectable by anyone who checks. (We say “tamper-evident” — the record proves whether it was altered, not that altering is impossible.)
Hash / fingerprint (SHA-256)
A short, fixed-length value computed from data. Any change to the data yields a completely different hash, so hashes act as fingerprints.
Hash chain
A sequence where each entry includes the previous entry’s hash, linking them so a change anywhere breaks the chain from that point on.
Entry / seq
One record in the ledger. seq is its sequence number, starting at 0 (genesis).
Genesis
The very first entry (seq 0). Verification always starts here — it is why the on-screen view begins at genesis.
Chain head
The hash of the most recent entry in view — the current “tip” of the chain.
Batch & Merkle root
Entries are grouped into batches (~100 events). A Merkle root is one fingerprint that summarizes a whole batch, so a single value can vouch for many entries.
Anchor
Publishing a batch’s Merkle root to a public log, creating independent proof it existed in that form at that time.
Sigstore / Rekor
An open-source, publicly-run transparency log. Tracelane anchors your batch roots here so the proof does not depend on trusting Tracelane.
logIndex
The position of an anchored entry within the public Rekor log — a coordinate that, with the log, locates the proof.
Checkpoint
The public log’s own signed statement of its current size and root. Your anchors are verified against it, offline.
Signature (Ed25519)
Your ledger’s batch roots are signed by a key unique to your workspace, so an anchor is bound to you.
Evidence pack
The complete exported ledger (NDJSON) plus the proofs needed to verify it independently.

10 · FAQ

Is “Verify integrity” just a demo?
No. It runs the real, open-source verifier in your browser over your real ledger. A green result is one you reproduced yourself, not a status Tracelane asserted.
Does verifying send my data anywhere?
No. The check is entirely local to your browser. Public-anchor proofs travel with your evidence, so even that check needs no live network call to Tracelane.
Why does the anchoring count seem stuck (e.g. “10”)?
The page verifies a preview of the first ~1,000 events. The anchor count reflects the batches inside that preview, not your whole ledger. Your complete set of anchors is in the export.
What decides batch size and how many batches I have?
Events are grouped into fixed-size batches of about 100 as they accrue; one anchor is published per batch. So the batch count grows one-per-~100-events, from genesis onward.
My ledger has millions of events — can the page show all of them?
The browser view is a verifiable preview by design (you can’t hash millions of rows in a tab). The complete chain is verified out-of-band via the export and the tlane verify CLI, which streams the entire ledger with no cap.
What should I do if verification fails?
Re-download a fresh export and verify again; most failures are a locally-edited/truncated file. If a clean export still fails, email support@tracelane.dev with the first failing seq — it’s handled as a potential integrity incident.
Can Tracelane secretly change my past records?
Not without it becoming detectable. That’s the whole point: an alteration breaks the hash chain and diverges from what’s already anchored in the public log.
Is the record in my local time?
All timestamps are shown in UTC and labeled as such, so records from different regions and viewers never disagree about when something happened.

11 · Getting help

Support: support@tracelane.dev — or use the in-product Support page (top navigation). We follow up by email.

For a verification failure, include the first failing seq shown on the Audit page and attach the exported ledger. That is everything we need to investigate.
